task.title: Weekly Meal Planner: spec the prototype for building into the app
task.description:
## Context for this repo (added when the story was filed, 2026-11-17)

This is the next piece of work after the current branches land (Bun, recipe model provider, Convex Auth 2.0, Render). The repo is named "meal-planner" but today the app (PerfectPlate) is a recipe and shopping manager; this story adds the weekly meal planning that name promises.

The owner's writeup below asks for a product and technical spec first, written from a standalone prototype. It was written without reference to this codebase, so when speccing, also record how each prototype feature maps onto what the app already has, and treat overlaps as open questions for the owner rather than deciding them:
- Accounts and per-user data already exist (Convex + Convex Auth email/password).
- Recipe import from a link or forwarded email already exists (server-side fetch, schema.org JSON-LD, model-structured ingredients), and it stores the method; the prototype stores ingredients only.
- Grocery lists already exist (built from saved recipes, grouped by store section, editable); the prototype derives one list per week from the plan.
- The model provider is configurable (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter) and paid for by the deployment owner; the prototype calls Claude on the viewer's own account.
- No Todoist integration and no nutrition data exist in the app today.

First step of the work is the spec described below, not implementation.

---

# Task: write a product and technical spec for the Weekly Meal Planner

You are writing a spec for turning an existing single-page prototype into a full-fledged app. Your first job is to document what the prototype does today, accurately and completely. Your second is to list the decisions a full app forces, as open questions for the owner. Do not design new features or pick a stack unprompted.

## Source of truth

The prototype is a single self-contained HTML file (vanilla JS, no framework, about 700 lines) published as a Claude artifact:
https://claude.ai/artifact/G9Ze96qvx2EXr1YvH9i7x3

Read the source before writing anything. Where this summary and the code disagree, the code wins; note the discrepancy. If you cannot open the artifact, ask the owner for the HTML export rather than specifying from this summary alone.

## Who it is for and why

One person planning his own lunches and dinners week by week. He does not plan breakfast. He tried todo apps, notepads and a calendar (too slow to capture and edit) and dedicated recipe apps (do too much). The value is speed of capture and a short path from plan to shopping list. Keep that bias in the spec: every feature below earned its place by removing typing.

## What exists today

### Plan view (default)
- One week at a time, seven rows, each with a lunch and a dinner slot. Previous/next week and "This week" navigation. Week start is a setting (Sat, Sun or Mon).
- A slot is unplanned or one of four types: Cook, Leftovers, Eat out, Skip. Pressing the selected type again clears the slot.
- Capture is keyboard-first: type a meal name and press Enter to jump to the next slot. In an untyped slot, text starting with "out", "leftovers" or "skip" sets the type; anything else is Cook. Names autocomplete from saved meals and past plans.
- Leftovers point at a cooked or eaten-out meal from the previous six days (can cross a week boundary), defaulting to the most recent. "Other leftovers" takes a free-text name instead.
- Pasting a recipe URL into a slot creates a Cook meal and imports the recipe (see Recipe import).
- Pasting a long description (over 80 characters) into an Eat out or Other leftovers slot has Claude name the meal and estimate its nutrition.
- Each slot shows calories and protein, ingredient count, a warning if details are missing, a Details link, and a link back to the recipe if there is one.
- Each day shows lunch + dinner calories and protein, a bar against the calorie target, and a count of meals not counted. A strip above shows slots planned out of 14, counts by type and average calories.
- A banner lists meals missing ingredients or nutrition, with one button to have Claude fill them all in.

### Saved meals
- A meal is identified by its normalized name. Renaming a slot means a different meal; there is no rename.
- Kinds: cooked, eaten out, leftovers. Fields: name, recipe yield in servings, ingredients (name, quantity, unit, aisle), per-serving nutrition (calories, protein, carbs, fat, saturated fat, fiber, sodium), a free-text description, source URL, and flags for whether the numbers are Claude's estimate or came from the recipe page.
- An editor dialog allows: editing every field; adding an ingredient from free text such as "2 lb chicken thighs"; filling in from a recipe link or pasted ingredient list; having Claude draft a recipe and nutrition, estimate nutrition only, or redraft; deleting the meal.
- Claude's recipe drafts lean toward the user's dietary targets and notes. Estimates are labelled as estimates everywhere.

### Recipe import
- From a link: the page's schema.org Recipe data is read (ingredients, yield, nutrition, title). Claude converts ingredient lines into shopping items (normalized name, numeric quantity, US grocery unit, aisle). Nutrition comes from the page when present, otherwise Claude estimates it.
- From pasted text: Claude extracts the same structure.
- Only ingredients are stored, never the method.
- Constraint in the prototype: the page cannot fetch websites, so links are read through a headless browser (Lightpanda) running as a local MCP server on the owner's computer. Link import therefore only works in the Claude desktop app on that machine. NYT Cooking was confirmed to expose the needed data without a login.

### Shopping list view
- Derived, not entered: built from the week's Cook slots. Portions for a cooked meal are 1 plus the number of leftover slots pointing at it. Ingredients scale by portions × people cooked for ÷ recipe yield.
- Same ingredient with the same unit is merged across meals. No unit conversion. Countable units round up to whole numbers; others show quarter fractions.
- Grouped by aisle: Produce, Meat & fish, Dairy & eggs, Bakery, Pantry, Frozen, Other.
- Per week: tick items already in the house, add extra items by hand, copy the remaining items as text.
- Todoist: a button sends unticked, not-yet-sent items to the owner's "Shopping" project. Each item goes to a section (his stores: Groceries, Costco, Pet Store, Asian Grocer / Other). There is a default store, a per-row override, and the override is remembered per ingredient. Tasks read "Ground turkey (2 lb)" with the meals in the description. Sent items are marked and skipped on later sends; the marks can be cleared. Sections are re-read from Todoist before each send. On an unconfirmed write the app does not retry and tells the user to check Todoist.

### Nutrition view
- Editable daily targets: calories, a flat calorie allowance for unplanned breakfast and snacks, protein minimum, fiber minimum, saturated fat maximum, sodium maximum. Blank means untracked.
- Priorities (Lower cholesterol, Lower sodium, More fiber, Higher protein) that prefill blank targets with common defaults, plus free-text notes. Both feed Claude's drafts and reviews.
- Calories-per-day chart stacked by macro with a target line, and the week's macro split.
- Day-by-day table for all seven nutrients with over/under/on-target markers and a weekly average. Document the exact threshold rules from the code.
- A short written review of the week by Claude on request, saved with its date.

### Settings
Week start day, number of people cooked for, list of saved meals.

### Storage
A per-artifact document store, owner-only: preferences, Todoist config, ingredient-to-store map, one document per day, one per saved meal, one per week's shopping-list state (ticks, extras, sent marks, review). Document the actual shapes from the code.

## Platform dependencies to call out

The prototype leans on Claude artifact capabilities that a standalone app must replace. For each, specify what it does today and what the replacement needs to provide:
- Document storage and single-owner access.
- Claude calls made from the page on the viewer's own account (recipe drafting, ingredient parsing, nutrition estimates, weekly review). Include the prompts and the expected JSON shapes as an appendix.
- The viewer's Todoist connector (two tools: list sections, add tasks).
- The local Lightpanda browser for reading recipe pages.

## Known gaps and untested areas

- Everything was tested against stand-ins for storage, Claude, Todoist and Lightpanda, not live services. Treat live behavior as unverified.
- Meal identity is the name; no rename, no merge of near-duplicates.
- No unit conversion when merging ingredients.
- Quantity changes after sending to Todoist are not synced; there is no two-way sync.
- No undo, no copy-a-week, no history view. All days are loaded at start with no pagination.
- Nutrition is estimated, breakfast is a flat number, and targets are generic defaults rather than advice.

## What to produce

1. **As-built functional spec**: every view, interaction and rule above, verified against the code, written so a developer could rebuild the same behavior. Include keyboard behavior and empty, loading and error states.
2. **Data model**: entities, fields, relationships and derived values (portions, shopping quantities, day totals, target status), with the formulas.
3. **Integrations**: Claude, Todoist and recipe fetching, with inputs, outputs, failure handling and user-facing error copy.
4. **Open questions for the owner**: do not answer these yourself. At minimum: target platforms; single user or household; accounts and sync; which AI provider and who pays for calls; server-side recipe fetching and its legal limits; Todoist auth; whether to keep meal identity by name; migration of the existing saved data.
5. **Out of scope**: things the prototype deliberately does not do.

Keep as-built behavior and proposals clearly separated. If you find a bug or an inconsistency in the code, list it in its own section instead of silently specifying the fixed behavior.
